**Where we are ahead:** the only Zig EtherNet/IP; typed, allocation-free codec of the full explicit stack (encap, CPF, EPATH, Message Router, Connection Manager incl. Large Forward Open, Logix tag services, Multiple Service Packet) validated against three third-party stacks and Wireshark; a browsable, tag-list-uploadable adapter that OpENer-style stacks do not give in library form for simulation. **Where we are behind:** no implicit Class 0/1 I/O engine (no cyclic producer/RPI/watchdog), no Template Object/UDT member decoding, no CIP Safety/Sync/Security, no PCCC, no Port/Connection objects on the adapter (→ *Backlog / deferred*, *What is deliberately not done*); the Assembly object is served for explicit messaging only (no implicit I/O).

## Design & invariants

Seven allocation-free layers, mirroring the protocol's own stacking
(encapsulation → CPF → CIP Message Router → Connection Manager → the Logix tag
services). Every wire struct uses explicit shifts and `std.mem.readInt`/
`writeInt` in its encode/decode rather than a `packed struct`, so the octet
layout never depends on Zig's bitfield-packing rules.

- **`encap` (Vol 2 ch. 2).** The length field counts the data **after** the
  24-octet header. It must account for *exactly* the octets present — this
  protocol has no checksum, so a length disagreement is the only signal that
  framing has gone wrong, and neither a short nor a long message is accepted;
  `decodePrefix` exists for the framer, which legitimately has the next message
  behind this one. `options` is *checked* to be zero rather than ignored: Vol 2
  §2-3.6 requires senders to zero it and receivers to reject anything else, and
  being strict is what stops a crafted message steering a future extension.
  `Framer` compacts on `feed`, refuses a message larger than its own storage
  (rather than waiting forever for octets that will never fit) and returns
  `null` until a whole message is present.

  **The `sockaddr_in` inside the identity and sockaddr items is network byte
  order in the middle of a little-endian message.** It is the single most
  common decoding mistake in this protocol and it does not fail loudly — port
  44818 read little-endian is 4783, which looks like a plausible port. It is
  owned in one place (`SocketAddress`) and bridged to `netaddr.Ip` there.

  **The `ListServices` name is not a fixed 16 octets.** The spec draws it that
  way; the reference target used for the goldens emits `"Communications\0"` —
  fifteen — and stops. The name is therefore "whatever is left in the item",
  which round-trips both shapes. A spec-literal decoder rejects real traffic.
- **`cpf`.** The structure is trivial and the rules over it are where
  implementations go wrong, so the rules are code: `validateDataOrder` requires
  at least two items, an address item first and a data item second, and refuses
  a connected address paired with unconnected data (or the reverse). Every walk
  bounds itself against the buffer rather than against the declared item count,
  so a peer that lies about the count cannot steer it out of bounds, and a
  declared count larger than the caller's item storage is an error rather than
  a silent truncation.

  **`SendRRData`/`SendUnitData` prefix the item list with a four-octet
  interface handle and a two-octet timeout; `ListIdentity` and friends do
  not.** Mixing those up shifts every item by six octets, which is why the
  envelope is a separate entry point (`decodeEnvelope`) and not a flag.

  **A connected data item begins with a two-octet sequence count that belongs
  to the item, not to CIP.** Handing it on to a CIP decoder shifts the service
  code by two and produces confident nonsense.
- **`epath` (Vol 1 App. C).** Four rules carry almost all of the bugs, and each
  is enforced rather than assumed: the path size is in **words** (so `words()`
  refuses an odd path instead of rounding); a 16/32-bit logical segment carries
  a pad octet in a *padded* path and not in a *packed* one (`padded` is an
  explicit parameter on both the iterator and the builder, never inferred); an
  ANSI Extended Symbol segment pads to even and **the pad is not part of the
  name** (`91 05 "SCADA" 00` is a five-character name); and array element
  indices are **Member ID** segments (`0x28`/`0x29`/`0x2A`), not attribute or
  instance segments.

  **Every legal spelling of the same path is preserved, and every illegal one
  is a typed error.** CIP leaves a decoder several ways to be silently wrong
  here, and all of them end in the same place: our stack and the peer disagree
  about which octets the frame was.

  - The decoded `Logical.format` is kept, because a peer may write instance 1
    as a 16-bit segment even though 8 bits would do.
  - A port segment's two escapes are kept as `Port.extended_size` /
    `Port.extended_port`, because both are legal for values that would fit
    without them (`11 01 <link> 00` is a legal spelling of `01 <link>`, and
    `0F 03 00 <link>` of `03 <link>`). Deriving the form from `link.len` and
    `port` instead **shrank a captured route path by two octets**, which shifts
    the path-size word count of everything downstream that rebuilds a route it
    received. `Builder.port` still picks the narrowest form for paths we
    originate; `Builder.portVerbatim` reproduces the one that arrived, and
    `Builder.segment` uses that.
  - **Every** alignment pad is required to be zero — the one after an odd
    symbolic or ANSI-symbol name, the one after an odd port segment, and the
    one between a 16/32-bit logical segment's type octet and its value. The
    spec fixes all four at zero, so a non-zero one means the path is
    misaligned; accepting one would let the decoder take 256 spellings of a
    path the encoder can write only one of. `Iterator.checkPad` is the single
    site, so a fifth pad cannot be added without one.

  Port segments pad relative to the **segment start**, not to the running
  offset, which only differs inside a packed path but differs silently there.
- **`cip`.** A reply sets bit 7 of the service code; `Reply` stores the service
  **stripped** and re-encodes it set, and `Request.decode` refuses a message
  with the bit set (and `Reply.decode` one without) rather than reading a
  reply's general status as a path size. `additional_status_size` is counted in
  words and is attacker-controlled — a count of 255 claims 510 octets that may
  not exist — so it is bounds-checked against the buffer.

  **`Multiple_Service_Packet`'s offsets are measured from the start of the
  count field.** Getting that wrong shifts every embedded request by two octets
  plus the table's width and decodes as garbage rather than failing, so both
  directions are asserted against captured traffic. `at(i)` additionally
  requires offsets to be non-decreasing and to point past the table, because an
  out-of-order table would otherwise produce overlapping or negative-length
  slices.

  **Service codes are only unique within an object class.** `0x52` is
  `Unconnected_Send` on class 6 and `Read Tag Fragmented` on a symbol object;
  `0x4E` is `Forward_Close` or `Read Modify Write Tag`. `Service` is therefore
  the *common* services only, the Logix and Connection Manager codes live in
  their own namespaces, and `Request.classCode()` (which reads the class
  segment out of the path) is what the dispatcher consults **before** the code.
- **`connmgr`.** The timeout is `2^(tick & 0x0F)` milliseconds × `ticks`, not a
  number of milliseconds — the everyday `5, 157` is 5024 ms. The upper bits of
  the tick octet are a priority field and must not enter the arithmetic.

  **The `Unconnected_Send` pad octet exists only when the embedded message's
  length is odd.** A decoder that always skips it (or never does) mis-locates
  the route path. **`Forward_Open` has no reserved octet after its
  connection-path size, while `Unconnected_Send` and `Forward_Close` both do**
  — this was found against captured traffic and is the difference between a
  connection that opens and one the target answers with a path-segment error.

  The 16-bit and 32-bit network connection parameters have **different bit
  layouts** (9-bit size with the flags above it, versus a full 16-bit size with
  the flags in the top half), not merely different widths;
  `ConnectionParameters` owns both and `toU16` returns null for a size the
  small form cannot express, which is what makes the choice of
  `Large_Forward_Open` mechanical rather than a guess.

  **The bits neither layout assigns are carried, not cleared.** The 16-bit word
  leaves bit 12 unassigned and the 32-bit word leaves bits 16-24 and bit 28
  (`ConnectionParameters.reserved_mask_16` / `_32`; cross-checked against
  Wireshark's CIP dissector, which maps exactly the complement of each). A
  sender is required to zero them and every captured frame does — but "the
  sender must zero it" is not "we may zero it for him": dropping them made the
  decode lossy and the encode unable to reproduce what had just been accepted,
  so a `Forward_Open` relayed through this module came out as different octets
  than went in. They are ignored on receipt rather than rejected, because
  refusing them would add a denial path on an unauthenticated listening surface
  for a field that changes nothing about the connection — the same treatment
  `ForwardOpen.reserved` already gives its three reserved octets.

  A `Forward_Close` matches on the `{connection serial, originator vendor,
  originator serial}` **triple**, not on a connection id — it does not carry
  one. Two originators that pick the same serial are told apart by their vendor
  id, which is why all three travel together everywhere.
- **`types`.** The type code is a **16-bit** little-endian value even though
  every elementary type fits in one octet. A structure reply sends `0x02A0`
  followed by a two-octet **structure handle** naming the UDT, and only then
  the member octets; a decoder that treats the handle as data is off by two for
  the whole tag. `date_and_time` (0xCF) is deliberately **not** given an
  element size: the published tables disagree about its width and guessing
  wrong silently mis-slices an array, so it is handed back as `.raw`.

  `Read Tag Fragmented`'s offset is in **octets**, not elements, so a caller
  resuming after a partial read advances by the octets it received.
  `Write Tag` orders its fields `{type, count, values}` and
  `Write Tag Fragmented` `{type, count, offset, values}`; swapping them writes
  plausible garbage. `partial_transfer` (0x06) is **not** an error — it is how
  a fragmented read says "there is more" — which is why `GeneralStatus.hasData`
  exists alongside `isSuccess`.
- **`tagpath`.** Logix's own name rules are checked, not assumed: a name starts
  with a letter or underscore, contains only letters, digits and underscores,
  is at most 40 characters, never contains two consecutive underscores and
  never ends in one. A silently-accepted bad name produces a request the
  controller answers with `path_segment_error`, which is a far worse debugging
  experience than a parse error. `Program:MainProgram` is **one** symbol
  segment including the colon, and the colon is only a scope prefix on the
  first component — anywhere else it is an illegal character.
- **`client`.** Everything a reply hands back points into the client's own
  receive buffer and is invalidated by the next call; that borrowed-slice
  contract is what keeps the client allocation-free, and it is stated at the
  top of the file and in the README. The transmit buffer is split so a request
  and the CPF envelope wrapping it never overlap.

  **Routing is an explicit choice, not a default that happens to work.** A
  ControlLogix chassis needs `Unconnected_Send` with a route path; a leaf
  device answers `path_segment_error` to exactly that message. `Routing` is
  therefore a tagged union with no "auto" case. `forwardOpen`/`forwardClose`
  temporarily force `.direct`, because a Connection Manager request is
  addressed to the *local* device and carries its own route — wrapping it again
  is the classic double-route bug.

  `readTagFragmented` loops on `partial_transfer` with two guards: a round
  ceiling, and a hard error if the target reports "more follows" while sending
  zero octets (which would otherwise loop forever).
- **`adapter`.** A pure function from one message to one message over
  caller-owned tag storage — no program execution, no scan cycle, no access
  control. The reply body is built in a scratch area and only then framed,
  rather than written past the header and framed in place: an in-place frame is
  a `@memcpy` of a region onto itself, which Zig's non-overlap contract does
  not permit. Nesting (`Unconnected_Send` inside `Unconnected_Send`,
  `Multiple_Service_Packet` inside itself) is **depth-capped**, because
  unbounded nesting is a stack-exhaustion primitive a hostile peer controls.

  **A `Multiple_Service_Packet` is budgeted before anything runs.** The whole
  offset table is validated first, so a bad later entry cannot follow an
  applied write in entry 0; every octet of the reply is budgeted up front (the
  reply header, the count and offset table, a minimal reply for each request
  still to come, `Config.max_reply`); an entry whose reply does not fit is
  answered `reply_data_too_large` alone, and every handler that changes state
  checks that its reply fits before it changes anything, so an overflow
  changes nothing (`adapter.zig`).

  The **TCP/IP Interface object** (class `0xF5`, instance 1; CIP Vol 2
  ch. 5-4) answers `Get_Attributes_All` (attributes 1 to 6 in order) and
  `Get_Attribute_Single` for the six attributes Vol 2 marks required:
  status, configuration capability, configuration control, physical link
  object (`20 F6 24 <n>`, or an empty path), interface configuration and host
  name. The values are the caller's (`Config.tcpip`, `null` withholds the
  object: `path_destination_unknown`); nothing is read from the OS. Encodings
  as OpENer (BSD-style licence, wire format read, nothing copied), EIPScanner
  and pycomm3 read them: an IPv4 address is a `UDINT` holding the address as a
  big-endian number (`192.168.1.1` is `01 01 A8 C0` on the wire), a `STRING`
  is a 16-bit length plus octets plus a pad octet when odd. Only instance 1
  exists (instance 0, the class level, answers `path_destination_unknown`); an
  attribute that is not served (7 and up, 0, anything above 16 bits) is
  `attribute_not_supported`; a missing attribute segment is
  `path_segment_error`; any other service is `service_not_supported`.
  `Set_Attribute_Single` is refused `attribute_not_settable` for every served
  attribute unless `Config.allow_tcpip_set`; with it, attributes 3, 5 and 6
  are settable (1, 2 and 4 stay read-only) and are only *recorded*: attribute 3
  takes method 0 to 2 and the DNS bit, attribute 5 needs the static method
  (`object_state_conflict` otherwise) and OpENer's address checks (set, not
  loopback, class A/B/C, not network/broadcast, contiguous mask, gateway on the
  same network) and a valid domain, attribute 6 an RFC 1123 label of 1 to 64
  octets; a short or long payload is `not_enough_data` / `too_much_data`, a bad
  value `invalid_attribute_value`; a successful 5 or 6 raises the status
  "interface configuration pending" bit and enabling the Set adds the
  "configuration settable" capability bit. Deviation from OpENer: it rejects the
  DNS-enable bit of attribute 3, Vol 2 allows it. Not served: the optional
  attributes 7 to 13 (safety network number, TTL, multicast, ACD, quick connect,
  encapsulation inactivity timeout).

  The **Ethernet Link object** (class `0xF6`, instance 1; Vol 2 ch. 5-5)
  serves the three required attributes, `Get_Attributes_All` (1 to 3 in
  order) and `Get_Attribute_Single`: interface speed (`UDINT`, Mbit/s),
  interface flags (`DWORD`: link active, full duplex, autonegotiation status,
  hardware fault) and the physical address (six octets, no length prefix),
  from `Config.ethernet_link` (defaults 100 Mbit/s, flags `0x0F`, a locally
  administered placeholder MAC; `null` withholds the object). The optional
  attributes (interface and media counters 4 and 5, interface control 6, type,
  state, admin state, label) are `attribute_not_supported`; instance 0 and any
  other instance `path_destination_unknown`. The object is read-only here and
  has no `Set_Attribute_Single` (`service_not_supported`), as OpENer builds it
  unless its interface-control option is on. Encodings as OpENer and the
  scanners (EIPScanner, pycomm3) read them.


  The **Assembly object** (class `0x04`, CIP Vol 1 ch. 5-5) is served from
  `Config.assemblies`, a list of caller-defined instances (`stdobj.Assembly`:
  instance id `1`-`65535`, the byte buffer, `writable`, a context pointer and
  optional `before_get` / `after_set` hooks); an empty list withholds the class
  as before (`path_destination_unknown`). Services as OpENer's
  `cipassembly.c` registers them (BSD-style licence; source read for behaviour
  only, nothing copied): `Get_Attribute_Single` and `Set_Attribute_Single`, and
  nothing else, so `Get_Attributes_All` on the class or an instance is
  `service_not_supported`. Instance attributes: 3 the data (octets as stored,
  `Get`; `Set` only on a `writable` instance), 4 its length as a `UINT` (`Get`
  only; a `Set` is `attribute_not_settable`); anything else `attribute_not_supported`.
  Class attributes (instance 0, `UINT` each): 1 revision `2`, 2 largest instance
  id, 3 number of instances, 6 highest class attribute (`7`), 7 highest instance
  attribute (`4`); 4 and 5 (optional lists) and everything else
  `attribute_not_supported`; `Set` on the class is `service_not_supported`.
  Refusals: unknown instance `path_destination_unknown` (`0x05`), unknown
  attribute `0x14`, `Set` on a non-writable instance `0x0E`, a `Set` whose length
  is not the buffer's exactly `0x13` (too short) or `0x15` (too long), checked in
  that order (attribute exists, settable, length). A missing attribute segment is
  `path_segment_error` (`0x04`), as on the other standard objects. The `after_set`
  hook runs after the octets are stored and a `false` answer is
  `invalid_attribute_value` (`0x09`) with the octets already replaced, which is
  what OpENer does (`AfterAssemblyDataReceived` after the `memcpy`); `before_get`
  lets the application refresh an input buffer before it is read. Buffers over
  65535 octets (the size is a `UINT`), instance 0 and a repeated id are not
  served (the first entry for an id wins). Deviation: OpENer has no per-instance
  writable flag (every instance is settable); the flag is this module's, so an
  input assembly can be read-only, answering `0x0E` as OpENer does for a
  non-settable attribute. The object is explicit messaging only: no implicit
  (Class 1) I/O engine, so assemblies are read and written on request only,
  not exchanged cyclically.


  It also answers enough for a browsing tool to **discover** its tags rather
  than be told them: the Program Name object (`0x64`, one `STRING`) and the
  Symbol Object's `Get_Instance_Attribute_List` (`0x6B` / `0x55`), which
  enumerates the bound tags with their names, CIP type codes, array dimensions
  and instance ids, continuing across replies through `partial_transfer` when
  the list does not fit one message. Those instance ids are also accepted as
  tag addresses (`20 6B 24 <id>` in place of a symbolic path), because a
  client switches to that form unprompted once the reported major revision is
  high enough — a device that hands ids out and then refuses them browses and
  cannot be read.

  The boundary is deliberate and narrow: no program-scoped tags; no other Symbol Object attribute or
  service. A struct-typed binding is listed only when it names its `Udt` (`TagBinding.udt`): the Template Object below
  describes it. One without a `udt` stays out of the list (readable by name). A
  one-element binding is advertised as a scalar, because `TagBinding` does not
  distinguish `DINT` from `DINT[1]`, and multi-dimensional arrays are
  advertised flat. It is a discoverable simulator, not a ControlLogix model.

Concurrency: `.single_owner` — one `Client`/`Adapter` owns one connection's
buffers, session handle and sequence counters; nothing is shared or global, and
any threading is the caller's.

Error policy: every decode entry point (`encap.decode`, `encap.Framer.next`,
`encap.Identity.decode`, `encap.Service.decode`, `cpf.decode`,
`cpf.decodeEnvelope`, `cpf.ConnectedData.decode`, `epath.Iterator.next`,
`cip.Request.decode`, `cip.Reply.decode`, `cip.MultipleService.at`,
`connmgr.UnconnectedSend.decode`, `connmgr.ForwardOpen.decode`,
`connmgr.ForwardClose.decode`, `types.decodeValue`, `types.TagData.decode`,
`types.WriteTagRequest.decode`, `tagpath.parse`, `Adapter.handle`) returns a
typed error on malformed input. Nothing panics, allocates or loops unboundedly.

## Verification

Run `scripts/modtest enip` (Debug and `-Doptimize=ReleaseFast`); `zig fmt --check modules/enip`. The suite is offline
except for three live tests that skip when no peer is set (README *Verify* has the variables).

### What is third-party-validated

The strongest evidence is not a hand-written vector but **real traffic between implementations that are not this
module**, a third independent decoder's reading of the same octets, and live round trips in both directions.

Oracles, all driven as black boxes only (to generate wire traffic, to act as a live peer, to be diffed against); no
third-party source was read as a design reference for them. Under CONVENTIONS §5 they are test oracles, so no
`NOTICE` entry is required (the README's `Provenance:` line records the one design reference):

1. **`cpppo`**, which ships an EtherNet/IP client and a simulated EtherNet/IP **server** (`python -m cpppo.server.enip`).
2. **`pycomm3`**, an independently written Logix driver, used as a second client and as a client against *our* adapter.
3. **Wireshark's `enip`/`cip` dissector**, reached through `rawshark` (`tshark` needs root to install).

Goldens (`src/goldens.zig`), each an assertion over byte-exact captured frames:

- **`table`**: both Python clients pointed at the cpppo server through an encapsulation-aware recording TCP proxy (and a
  UDP one for discovery); every message that crossed the wire was logged as hex. Four assertions run over the table:
  every frame decodes at the encapsulation layer and re-encodes to the identical octets; every data-carrying frame's CPF
  envelope decodes, passes `validateDataOrder` and re-encodes identically; every CIP request and reply re-encodes
  identically, every request's EPATH is rebuilt from its decoded segments through `epath.reencode` (so the encoder is
  what is checked, not a memcpy), and every `Unconnected_Send`, `Forward_Open`, `Large_Forward_Open` and `Forward_Close`
  body is rebuilt from its decoded fields; and a coverage assertion fails if the table stops containing any
  encapsulation command, CPF item type, CIP service or routing shape the module models, traffic from both client
  stacks, a CIP-layer error reply and an encapsulation-layer error reply. The capture includes routed and unrouted tag
  services, a `Multiple_Service_Packet`, both fragmented services, a `Forward_Open` and a `Large_Forward_Open` from the
  other stack, connected `SendUnitData` exchanges, `ListIdentity` over TCP and over UDP, and two encapsulation error
  replies whose body is zero octets (the shape that breaks a decoder insisting on a CPF envelope).
- **`adapter_table`**: `pycomm3` and `cpppo` driven as real independent clients against our own `Adapter.init(.{}, &tags)`
  through the same recording proxy, so the listening surface has a foreign oracle and not only our own `Client` reading
  its own replies. Besides the decode/re-encode assertion, every captured request is replayed through a fresh
  `Adapter.handle`, in capture order, and the reply must equal the captured reply byte for byte: the bytes were accepted
  by the clients' own parsers at capture time. A value no self round trip pins (the first connection id the adapter
  issues) is what this table catches.
- **`discovery_table`, `discovery_instance_table`**: a stock `pycomm3.LogixDriver` (no subclass, no tag table supplied)
  browsing our adapter: Program Name object, tag-list upload, then reads and writes of tags it learned only from that
  upload. Two sessions differ only in the major revision the adapter reports, because that changes what the client asks
  for: at `revision_major = 1` symbolic addressing, at `revision_major = 21` symbol instance addressing (`20 6B 24 <id>`
  and no name). Both are replayed through a fresh `Adapter.handle` byte for byte; the tag-list continuation test fails if
  a `partial_transfer` is answered `success`.
- **`stdobj_table`**: a stock `pycomm3` `CIPDriver.generic_message` reading and writing the TCP/IP Interface and Ethernet
  Link objects over loopback against the adapter, replayed byte for byte. pycomm3 accepted every reply and decoded the
  speed, the host name and the pad octet; it has no typed view of these objects, and its `Struct` declarations for
  attributes 4 and 5 and its `Array(USINT, 6)` for the MAC did not decode, a property of those declarations and not a
  disagreement about the octets.
- **`assembly_table`**: the same client reading both instances and the class attributes of the Assembly object, writing
  the writable one and provoking every refusal; replayed byte for byte. pycomm3 accepted every reply and named every
  refusal correctly.

The identity in the goldens is anonymised (length-preserving substitutions of the simulator's product name and serial
number, applied everywhere they appear, so no length or offset moves); a test asserts the substitution, so an
unanonymised capture pasted in fails.

**Wireshark cross-check** (one-off, not part of the suite): the client-direction frames were written into a pcap and
dissected with `rawshark -s -d proto:enip`; `enip.command`, `enip.cpf.typeid`, `cip.service` (including the services inside
an `Unconnected_Send` and a `Multiple_Service_Packet`), `cip.genstat` and `cip.symbol` were compared field by field with
this module's reading, with no mismatch. The suite does not depend on Wireshark being installed.

**Live round trips** (gated on environment variables, `SKIPPED:` and pass otherwise, `root.zig`):

- `ENIP_TEST_SERVER`: our client against a live target: `RegisterSession`, `ListIdentity`/`ListServices`, an INT write
  with read-back, an array read, `Read Tag Fragmented`, a two-tag `Multiple_Service_Packet`, a missing tag refused,
  `UnRegisterSession`.
- `ENIP_TEST_CONNECTED`: `Forward_Open`, three `SendUnitData` exchanges with incrementing sequence counts,
  `Forward_Close`.
- `ENIP_TEST_LISTEN`: real third-party clients against our adapter: the cpppo client (`ListIdentity`, `ListServices`,
  array reads, a write with read-back) and pycomm3 (`ListIdentity`, an unconnected `Get_Attributes_All`, and a
  `Large_Forward_Open`, a connected `Get_Attribute_Single` and a `Forward_Close`), all accepted by their own decoders.

**A divergence recorded**: the cpppo target refuses a `Read Tag Fragmented` that is not wrapped in an `Unconnected_Send`,
answering an encapsulation-layer `0x0008`. It is a limitation of that target, not of this module: the cpppo client
driving the same target unrouted gets the identical refusal, and our routed request is byte for byte what the cpppo
client sends.

### What is self-derived

- **16- and 32-bit logical segments and their pad octet.** No captured frame contains one (every captured path uses
  8-bit class, instance, attribute and member segments). The forms follow the documented layout and are round-trip and
  hostile-input tested; the `tagpath` tests that produce them (`Big[300]`, `Big[70000]`) are self-derived too.
- **The packed (unpadded) EPATH form.** Modelled from the specification and round-trip tested.
- **The `Unconnected_Send` pad octet for an odd embedded message.** Every captured embedded message was even-length, so
  the pad is unit-tested against the documented rule.
- **Port segments beyond `01 00`.** The extended-link-address form (`0x10 | port`, size, address) and the extended-port
  escape (`0x0F`, 16-bit port) are decoded and re-encoded from the documented layout.
- **Network segments and the electronic key.** Decoded and re-encoded from the documented layouts.
- **Structure (UDT) reads.** The `0x02A0` + handle shape is implemented from the specification; a stock `pycomm3`
  (1.2.16) reads structures of the simulator, with their templates, through `tools/udt_serve.zig` + `tools/udt_oracle.py`
  (nested types, arrays, handle; external, live, not a capture). The member layout and the template name's `;n` suffix
  are what pycomm3's parser accepts; they are not checked against a controller's own bytes.
- **Sequenced Address items and the sockaddr-info items.** Codecs only; implicit I/O was never exercised.
- **CIP data types beyond INT, DINT, REAL and SHORT_STRING.** Round-trip tested against their documented codes and widths.
- **`Get_Attribute_List` / `Set_Attribute_List`.** Encoders and a reply iterator built from the specification.
- **The oracle target is a simulator, not real hardware.** No ControlLogix, CompactLogix, MicroLogix, PowerFlex or
  third-party adapter was available; quirks of real firmware (connection-resource limits, the real `0x6B` tag list,
  optimised/atomic tag layout, chassis routing through a real communication module, a tag write landing mid-scan) are
  not covered.

### Fuzz and hostile input

Fuzz harnesses (`src/fuzz_test.zig` holds the shared plumbing; the bodies sit beside their corpora) run by testkit's
deterministic driver as `ENIP_FUZZ=<runs>[,<first seed>]`, with a fixed seed loop and reach counters in every test run;
each asserts "typed error or valid result, never a panic and never a hang":

- `encap.decode` (anything that decodes re-encodes to the identical octets and its `total_len` equals the input length),
  `encap.Framer` fed arbitrary chunks (a guard fails the test if `next` returns a message without consuming input), and
  the `Identity`, `Service` and `SocketAddress` decoders;
- `cpf.decode` and `cpf.decodeEnvelope`, with every typed view walked over every decoded item;
- `epath.reencode`, `findLogical`, `findSymbol`, `countSegments` and a packed iteration with a step guard;
- `cip.Request`/`cip.Reply`, `cip.MultipleService` (every slice handed out lies inside the payload) and
  `cip.AttributeListIterator`;
- `connmgr`'s four decoders, `types.decodeValue`, `TagData`, `WriteTagRequest`, `WriteTagFragmentedRequest`;
- `tagpath.parse` (anything that parses encodes to a legal even-length EPATH that re-encodes exactly);
- `Adapter.handle` over arbitrary messages, half with a session already open, anything the adapter emits required to be a
  legal encapsulation message; `Client.readTag` against an arbitrary reply.

Explicit hostile-input tests (not fuzz) cover: an encapsulation length disagreeing with the payload in both directions,
a truncated header, non-zero options, a message larger than the framer's storage; a CPF item count that overruns its
storage, an item length past the buffer, trailing octets after the last item, a data item first, a connected address
paired with unconnected data and the reverse, a connected data item too short for its sequence count; an EPATH segment
whose size runs past the path, a zero-length symbolic segment, an odd symbolic segment with its pad missing, a dirty pad
octet on all four padded shapes, both non-canonical port spellings re-encoded verbatim, reserved logical types and
formats; a request path size that overruns, a reply with the request bit and the reverse, a dirty reserved octet, an
additional-status count that overruns; a `Multiple_Service_Packet` offset table pointing outside the payload or into
itself, descending offsets; `Unconnected_Send` and `Forward_Open` sizes that overrun, dirty reserved and pad octets,
captured `Forward_Open` bodies re-encoded with a reserved network-parameter bit set; a string length prefix past the
data, a type code contradicting the data length, a structure reply missing its handle, an out-of-range element index;
roughly twenty-five malformed tag paths; and hostile encapsulation messages driven straight through `Adapter.handle`.

- **Audit:** the card's `**Audit:**` line is the current score, cumulative over the last whole-module mutation run and
  the delta runs after it.

## Threat model

EtherNet/IP is an **unauthenticated, unencrypted** protocol by design: anyone
with a path to TCP 44818 can enumerate a device, read and write every tag it
exposes, and reboot it. This module's job is therefore robustness and
containment, not confidentiality or integrity against an active attacker:

- Hostile or corrupt bytes from a misbehaving controller, a hostile client or a
  MITM resolve to typed errors at every decode entry point.
- No allocation anywhere, and every buffer is caller-supplied and bounded, so a
  hostile peer cannot drive memory growth. Nesting inside `Unconnected_Send`
  and `Multiple_Service_Packet` is depth-capped so it cannot drive *stack*
  growth either.
- **Time is bounded too, once `setReadTimeout` is set.** `TcpTransport`'s
  read timeout is a deadline for the *whole* encapsulation message on the
  monotonic clock, not for its first octet, so a peer that sends part of a
  message and goes quiet (slowloris) costs the reading thread — the adapter's
  included — at most that long, and the read fails with `ReadFailed`. With no
  timeout set a read blocks indefinitely, by design; a server facing untrusted
  peers sets one.
- **`Reset` (service 0x05) is implemented and is dangerous.** On the Identity
  object it reboots the device; there is no authentication step in front of it
  anywhere in the protocol. It is exposed because a diagnostic tool and a fleet
  simulator both need it and pretending it does not exist does not make a plant
  safer, but: nothing in this module calls it implicitly, it is spelled out in
  full at its call site, and the `Adapter` **refuses it unless `allow_reset` is
  explicitly set**.
- **Writing a tag on a running machine changes what that machine is doing.**
  There is no "safe" write in this protocol and no confirmation step; the
  module offers no guardrail beyond making every write an explicit call.
- **`ListIdentity` broadcast is a network-wide enumeration primitive.** It is
  exactly what an attacker's first packet on an OT segment looks like. Do not
  run a discovery sweep across a segment you do not own.
- **CIP Security (Volume 8) is not implemented.** Deployments must put
  transport security underneath — a VPN, or a CIP-Security-capable stack —
  and callers should hand the `Transport` seam an already-secured stream,
  exactly as the repo's BYO-TLS rule (CONVENTIONS §2) prescribes.
- The adapter is a **simulator, not a controller**: it executes no program,
  enforces no access level and models no safety function. Do not put one on a
  network where something might mistake it for real equipment.
- **The client's reply checks are the references' level, not stricter.** Replies are tied to requests by the session
  handle, the connection sequence count and the strict one-request-one-reply stream order; see *What is deliberately not
  done* for the checks left out on purpose and their survey.

## What is deliberately not done

- **CIP Safety (Volume 5).** Not implemented, and deliberately not: a safety protocol implemented casually is worse than
  none.
- **CIP Security (Volume 8)**, EtherNet/IP over TLS/DTLS, the security profiles and the certificate management objects.
  Transport security goes underneath (see *Threat model*).
- **DeviceNet and ControlNet ports.** Only the EtherNet/IP adaptation is built; port segments can name another port so a
  route through a gateway can be expressed, but nothing here speaks those link layers.
- **Multiple concurrent outstanding requests.** The client performs one request/reply exchange per call, as every
  explicit-messaging driver does in practice.
- **Reconnection, retry and keepalive.** A transport failure is surfaced; a production deployment wires reconnection
  into its own supervisor.
- **Reply matching beyond the session handle and the sequence count.** `Client.sendConnectedCip` does not compare the
  reply's connected-address item id with the connection's `t_to_o_id`, and `Client.sendCip` does not check that the reply
  service is the request's service with bit 7 set. Surveyed against the references (behaviour only): pycomm3 (the
  reference client, MIT) parses the reply's service and status from fixed offsets and compares neither the service nor
  the connected-address id; EIPScanner (MIT) reads the reply service into the response without comparing it and reads no
  connection id on the explicit path; libplctag (MPL-2.0, source read for behaviour only) checks the reply service only
  inside each typed tag handler and logs the connected-address id without comparing it; cpppo is copyleft and was not
  read. So there is no majority for either check. A connected reply is tied to its request by the CPF sequence count
  (`SequenceMismatch`, `client.zig`) and every reply by the session handle (`SessionMismatch`, `client.zig`) and
  the one-request-one-reply stream order, so the stray-reply window equals the references'. A check on `sendCip` would
  also have to special-case `Unconnected_Send`, whose success reply carries the embedded service. Revisit only if a
  consumer shows a target that answers out of order. Related, also unchecked: `Client.forwardOpen` takes the connection
  serial from the reply instead of comparing the originator triple (`client.zig`), and `multipleServices` accepts
  fewer embedded replies than requests, returning the smaller count (`client.zig`).
- **`Timeout.fromMilliseconds(0)` returns null** (`connmgr.zig`): zero ticks is not a timeout the function will
  encode. The references do not convert milliseconds at all: they send fixed non-zero raw pairs (pycomm3
  `PRIORITY`/`TIMEOUT_TICKS` `0x0A`/`0x05`, libplctag `AB_EIP_SECS_PER_TICK`/`AB_EIP_TIMEOUT_TICKS` `0x0A`/`0x0E`) or
  take the raw tick pair from the caller (EIPScanner's `ConnectionParameters`, default 0), so there is no reference
  behaviour for 0 to follow. Kept for predictability: a caller that wants a deadline gets one at or above what it asked
  for, a zero request gets `null` instead of a silently different value, and the raw pair stays available through the
  struct fields. Pinned by the test `timeouts: the exponent is the low four bits and every encoding edge is found`.

## Backlog / deferred

- **Implicit I/O connection engine (Class 0/1, UDP 2222).** The Sequenced Address item (`0x8002`) and the Sockaddr Info
  items (`0x8000`/`0x8001`) encode and decode and `Forward_Open` carries the parameters an I/O connection needs, but
  there is no cyclic producer, no RPI timer, no connection watchdog, no sequence-number gap detection, no multicast group
  management and no Run/Idle header handling. Large (a cyclic scheduler with an injected clock); fits CONVENTIONS §2 if
  kept clock-agnostic. The single largest thing missing.
- **Connection watchdogs and timeout supervision.** `connection_timeout_multiplier` is carried on the wire and honoured by
  neither side; there is no timer anywhere in the module and a connection is closed only by a `Forward_Close` or a dead
  transport. Part of the implicit engine above.
- **CIP Sync / time synchronisation (Volume 2 ch. 7, IEEE 1588).** Not implemented.
- **PCCC encapsulation (`Execute PCCC`, 0x4B)** for legacy SLC/PLC-5 targets. Named, not implemented.
- **Adapter object coverage.** The adapter serves the Identity, Program Name (`0x64`), Symbol (`0x6B`), TCP/IP Interface
  (`0xF5`), Ethernet Link (`0xF6`) and, when `Config.assemblies` is non-empty, Assembly (`0x04`) objects and no other
  class. The Message Router, Connection, Port (`0xF4`) and Connection Configuration objects are named in `ClassCode` and
  not implemented on the target side (a client can address any of them with the generic attribute services).

## Template Object and user-defined types

`Config.udts` (`adapter.Udt`: template instance `id` 1..4095, `name`, structure `handle`, `size`, `members`) makes the adapter serve the **Template Object** (class 0x6C, one instance per type): `Get_Attribute_List` (0x03) answers attributes 1 (structure handle, UINT), 2 (member count, UINT), 4 (definition size in 32-bit words, UDINT) and 5 (structure size in octets, UDINT) as count, then per attribute id + status + value (0x14 and no value for one not served); `Read Template` (0x4C on this class, where it is Read Tag on a symbol) returns the definition from `offset` for `count` octets, as `partial_transfer` when the reply cannot hold them. The definition is one 8-octet descriptor per member (`UINT info` = array length, `UINT type` = the symbol type word, `UDINT offset`; an array sets bit 13, a nested type is `0x8000 | template id`), then the template name with the `;n` suffix and the member names, each NUL-terminated, padded with NULs so that `length + 23` is a whole number of words (a driver reads `4 * words - 23` octets). `TagBinding.udt` marks a structure tag: the Symbol Object lists it with the symbol type word `0x8000 | id`, and Read Tag answers `0x02A0` + the handle + the octets. Members are atomic types, arrays of them and nested types; strings and BOOL bit members are not modelled (give the host `SINT`/`DINT`). Checked live against `pycomm3` 1.2.16 (`tools/udt_oracle.py` against `tools/udt_serve.zig`).

## Anchoring

**Anchor grade:** class A · oracle EXTERNAL

- **Class A** — wire/interop format — other implementations must byte-agree with it.
- **Oracle EXTERNAL** — published vectors, goldens captured from a foreign implementation, or a test run against a live foreign peer.

**What the tests actually contain.** 61 goldens captured from real traffic between 3rd-party stacks + live round trips
